body:
Meaning of modernism in architecture

Modernism is a broad architectural approach that became especially influential during the 20th century. Instead of simply reproducing the decorative forms of earlier historical styles, modernist architects explored new ways of arranging buildings and using materials to meet contemporary needs.

Modernist buildings commonly emphasise function, geometrical forms, structural clarity and relatively simplified surfaces. Materials such as reinforced concrete, steel and glass made new types of buildings possible. However, modernism is not defined by one material, and modernist buildings are not necessarily without ornament or local identity.

In India, the design of modern buildings also had to respond to climate, social life, available materials and institutional requirements. Architects experimented with shaded spaces, courtyards, terraces and other features that connected modern construction with local conditions.

Chandigarh: a major planned city after Independence

Chandigarh was developed as a new capital city after Independence and Partition. It became an important example of modernist town planning in India.

The original planning team

The first planning work was undertaken by Albert Mayer and Matthew Nowicki. Their proposal included curving roads and neighbourhood units with housing, markets and open spaces.

Following Nowicki's death, the planning assignment passed to a new team in 1951, led by Le Corbusier, whose full name was Charles-Édouard Jeanneret.

Le Corbusier worked with important collaborators, including Pierre Jeanneret, Jane Drew and Maxwell Fry. Indian architects and planners also participated in the project.

Le Corbusier was the principal architect and planner associated with the executed modernist design of Chandigarh, but he was not the first person to prepare a plan for the city. The earlier Mayer–Nowicki contribution must be distinguished from the later Le Corbusier-led work.

Sectors and urban organisation

The Chandigarh plan organised the city into sectors, which functioned as neighbourhood units with their own facilities. The formal planning principles included an organised road system, open spaces and the distribution of residential and civic functions.

The Chandigarh Administration describes a typical sector as approximately 800 m by 1200 m. Major roads form its boundaries, while access to houses is arranged through the internal circulation system rather than direct entry from the surrounding high-speed roads.

The sector system illustrates the difference between planning a neighbourhood and designing one particular building.

Chandigarh Capitol Complex

Le Corbusier's Capitol Complex contains major governmental buildings, including the Secretariat, Legislative Assembly and High Court. The complex is a well-known expression of modernist architecture through its monumental concrete forms, strong geometry and organisation of public space.

The Chandigarh Capitol Complex forms the Indian component of the transnational UNESCO World Heritage property The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier, an Outstanding Contribution to the Modern Movement, inscribed in 2016.

The UNESCO designation applies to the designated Capitol Complex component within the larger international property. It should not be interpreted as an inscription of the entire city of Chandigarh.

Gandhinagar: Gujarat's planned capital

Gandhinagar is a major Indian example of a planned capital city developed after Independence. Its planning is associated with the chief architect and town planner H. K. Mewada, also written as Hargovind Mewada, and his colleague Prakash M. Apte.

Mewada and Apte had gained experience with the Chandigarh project. Their work on Gandhinagar reflects the adaptation of modern planning principles to the requirements of Gujarat's capital.

The city's organisation includes numbered roads, planned sectors, institutional areas and substantial green spaces. Its layout provides a useful contrast with the densely built historic neighbourhoods of old Ahmedabad.

The municipal account identifies 1970 as the year by which Gandhinagar's initial city infrastructure had been completed.

Chandigarh: Le Corbusier-led planning team from 1951, following the earlier Mayer–Nowicki proposal.
Gandhinagar: H. K. Mewada and Prakash M. Apte.
Both are planned cities, but they are not correctly attributed to the same principal designers.

Modern architecture in Ahmedabad

Ahmedabad contains important examples of post-Independence modern architecture. Its institutions and industrial development attracted architects who experimented with modern forms while responding to local conditions.

Le Corbusier and Ahmedabad

Le Corbusier designed several notable buildings in Ahmedabad during the 1950s.

The Ahmedabad Textile Mill Owners' Association Building, commonly known as ATMA House or the Mill Owners' Association Building, is a major example. Its concrete framework, geometric appearance and carefully arranged shading elements demonstrate the use of modern architecture in response to strong sunlight and the need for ventilation.

Other important works associated with Le Corbusier in Ahmedabad include Sanskar Kendra, a city museum building, and Villa Shodhan, a private residence.

These Ahmedabad buildings illustrate modern architecture, but they are not the Indian component of the 2016 UNESCO serial property. That component is the designated Chandigarh Capitol Complex.

Louis Kahn and the Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad

The historic campus of the Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad is associated with the architect Louis I. Kahn.

Kahn began work on the project in 1962, and the foundation-related ground-breaking ceremony took place on 9 September 1964. The old campus is particularly recognised for its monumental red-brick buildings and strong geometrical forms, including circles and arches.

Balkrishna V. Doshi helped connect the institution with Kahn and served as a consulting architect on the project. Therefore, Kahn was the principal designer of the historic campus, while Doshi had an important associated role.

Balkrishna Doshi and Sangath

Balkrishna V. Doshi was an important Indian modernist architect who developed an architectural approach sensitive to Indian social and climatic conditions.

His Sangath studio in Ahmedabad, completed in 1980, is known for its vaulted roofs, landscaped setting and use of spaces designed to moderate heat and support interaction.

Doshi was also closely associated with the School of Architecture established in Ahmedabad in 1962, which later became part of CEPT University. He received the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2018.

Important architect and work associations

Architect or planning teamImportant workPlace
Le Corbusier-led teamModernist master plan and Capitol ComplexChandigarh
H. K. Mewada and Prakash M. AptePlanned capital cityGandhinagar
Le CorbusierATMA House and Sanskar KendraAhmedabad
Louis I. KahnHistoric IIM Ahmedabad campusAhmedabad
Balkrishna V. DoshiSangathAhmedabad

Modernism compared with colonial revival styles

Neo-classical and Gothic Revival buildings commonly draw their visual identity from recognisable historical European forms. Indo-Saracenic buildings deliberately combine selected traditional forms. Modernist architecture places stronger emphasis on the arrangement of spaces, the functions of the building, modern materials and simplified geometrical expression.

The distinction is not absolute. A modernist building may respond to historic local traditions without copying their decorative appearance. For example, ATMA House uses modern concrete construction while addressing the practical problem of sunlight and air movement in Ahmedabad.

Prelims focus

  • Chandigarh's earlier planning team included Albert Mayer and Matthew Nowicki.
  • Le Corbusier's team took charge of the Chandigarh project in 1951.
  • Chandigarh's sectors are approximately 800 m by 1200 m.
  • The Chandigarh Capitol Complex is part of a UNESCO World Heritage property inscribed in 2016.
  • Gandhinagar was planned principally by H. K. Mewada and Prakash M. Apte.
  • Trap: The historic IIM Ahmedabad campus is chiefly associated with Louis Kahn, not Le Corbusier or Balkrishna Doshi as its principal designer.

[Chandigarh Administration, Historical Background, Planner; Chandigarh Administration, Edict of Chandigarh, Sectors; Ministry of Culture, Government of India, The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier, an Outstanding Contribution to the Modern Movement, Chandigarh, 2016; Gandhinagar Municipal Corporation, History; Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, Heritage City, ATMA House and Villa Shodhan; Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad Archives, Louis Kahn and the Campus Architecture; Pritzker Architecture Prize, Balkrishna Doshi, biography and selected works; official sources consulted 23 November 2026.]

body:
Meaning of adaptive reuse

Adaptive reuse is the process of giving an existing building a new function while retaining significant features of its architectural or historical character. It is especially relevant when a building has heritage value but its original use is no longer required or is no longer practical.

For example, a historic residence may be adapted into a hotel, cultural institution or another suitable use. The building continues to serve a purpose, while important features of its earlier design remain recognisable.

Adaptive reuse is not limited to colonial buildings. It can apply to older houses, warehouses, industrial structures, public institutions and other buildings from different historical periods.

Adaptive reuse and other conservation terms

Several terms are related but must not be treated as synonyms.

TermMain meaningKey distinction
PreservationProtecting significant existing historic material and characterDoes not necessarily require a new function
RepairCorrecting damage or deteriorationMay leave the original use unchanged
RestorationReturning significant features towards a documented earlier conditionConcerns the condition and appearance of historic features
Adaptive reuseIntroducing a compatible new functionChanges the use while retaining heritage significance

These activities can occur together. A building may be repaired and restored before it is adapted to a new use. However, a building that has merely been repainted or repaired has not necessarily undergone adaptive reuse.

Why adaptive reuse is useful

Historic buildings may lose their original purpose because institutions move, families relocate or commercial activities change. If such buildings remain unused, they may suffer neglect and deterioration.

A compatible new use can help maintain a building by providing an ongoing reason for its occupation, care and maintenance. Reusing an existing structure can also preserve a visible connection between a place and its history.

Nevertheless, not every new use is appropriate. A proposed function may require alterations that damage significant historic features or change the building's character too extensively. Successful adaptive reuse therefore involves finding a reasonable balance between continued use and heritage preservation.

Basic considerations when reusing a historic building

  • Identify significant features: Understand which parts of the building contribute most to its historical or architectural character.
  • Select a compatible function: Choose a new use that can be accommodated without destroying those important features.
  • Retain recognisable character: Preserve important façades, spaces, structural features and decorative elements wherever appropriate.
  • Make necessary adaptations carefully: Provide facilities required for the new function while limiting unnecessary damage to historic material.
  • Maintain the building: Continued occupation should be accompanied by ongoing care rather than treated as a one-time alteration.

These are general principles for understanding the concept. The precise requirements for an individual building depend on its condition, significance and intended use.

House of MG, Ahmedabad: an example of adaptive reuse

The House of MG provides a clear Gujarat example. It originated as the residence of the Mangaldas Girdhardas family, whose members were associated with Ahmedabad's textile industry.

The original mansion was built in 1904, and an additional wing followed in 1924. The façades display Neo-classical architectural features.

As members of the family moved away, parts of the property became neglected or were used for other purposes. A later conservation and conversion effort gave part of the property a new function as a heritage hotel. The House of MG opened in 2007, and another restored wing was subsequently incorporated by 2014.

This example demonstrates two ideas at once. The building's original architectural character can still be described as Neo-classical, while its later conversion from a family residence into a hotel is an example of adaptive reuse.

Gujarat's wider built-heritage context

Ahmedabad contains buildings from several different periods. The historic walled city is particularly known for traditional houses, pols, gateways, streets and other features associated with its earlier urban development.

A pol is a traditional residential neighbourhood or street organisation, commonly associated with closely arranged houses and community spaces in old Ahmedabad. Such urban forms are different from the planned sectors of modern Gandhinagar.

The Historic City of Ahmadabad was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2017. Its importance includes the historical organisation of neighbourhoods and traditional domestic architecture.

The UNESCO inscription concerns the historic city as a heritage property. It should not be confused with a designation of Gandhinagar as a heritage city, nor does it mean that the entire historic city represents colonial architecture.

How to distinguish the complete subtopic

The six concepts can be recognised through the particular question each answers.

  • Neo-classical: Does the building show classical symmetry, columns and monumental proportions?
  • Gothic Revival: Does the building prominently use pointed arches, steep roofs, towers and medieval-inspired ornament?
  • Indo-Saracenic: Does the building combine Indian forms such as domes, chhatris and jalis with European design approaches?
  • Town planning: How are roads, residential areas, institutions and open spaces organised across a settlement?
  • Modernism: Does the building emphasise contemporary functions, simplified geometric forms and modern construction approaches?
  • Adaptive reuse: Has an existing building acquired a compatible new function while retaining important heritage features?

A place or building may illustrate more than one of these ideas. For instance, the House of MG illustrates both Neo-classical architectural character and adaptive reuse. Chandigarh illustrates both modernist architecture and planned urban development.

Prelims focus

  • Adaptive reuse gives an existing building a new compatible function while retaining its significant heritage character.
  • Repair and restoration do not, by themselves, establish that adaptive reuse has occurred.
  • House of MG, Ahmedabad, originated as a family residence in 1904 and opened as a heritage hotel in 2007.
  • Its Neo-classical architecture and later adaptive reuse are separate but compatible descriptions.
  • The Historic City of Ahmadabad was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2017.
  • Trap: Historic Ahmedabad's traditional pols must not be confused with the planned modern sectors of Gandhinagar.

[Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, Heritage City, House of MG, history, restoration and architectural description; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Historic City of Ahmadabad, Description and Outstanding Universal Value, property 1551; Gandhinagar Municipal Corporation, History; official sources consulted 23 November 2026.]
